full_text:
Interviewer:	The questions that I’ve got today are mainly about how the placement’s going and how you think it relates to the course that you’re doing at University as well. So when did you start the placement?

Subject:	About July.

Interviewer:	And when do you finish?

Subject:	July.

Interviewer:	So you’ve got a bit of a break before you go back to University. Can you tell me a bit about the company and what they do?

Subject:	 [Company] used to be based [company] and [company] took over [company] a few years ago so most people still think they work at [company]. And basically my division is Energy and we make cable accessories etc. So that’s like working basically for utility companies, electrical companies, and doing stuff like making joints and conductors, break outs, things like that.

Interviewer:	Okay. How useful do you think that your degree has been so far to the work that you’re currently doing?

Subject:	Certain modules very useful. Stuff like the materials module we did was very useful because the work I’ve done has mostly been reformulating, like, rubbers and things and modules like Thermo have been useful to the work that I’ve been doing but that’s because of the projects that I’ve been working on so the other guys here have found different things useful.

Interviewer:	Yeah. Okay. Is there anything particular that you wish that you had learnt before you started the placement that would have been useful?

Subject:	A more in-depth knowledge of material would have helped but we’ve been taught it. They basically looked at what we already knew and built on it. So it would have helped just because we wouldn’t have had to learn so much in the first couple of months. I guess wherever you go you’re going to be thrown in at the deep end and you learn a lot to start off with.

Interviewer:	Yes. Okay. Where you taught anything about health & safety at Uni?

Subject:	I wouldn’t say in particular, it comes up, but it comes up as you need to know it rather than it’s forced on you, obviously if you go into a workshop at Uni the health & safety implications, you know, you’re shown them before you start any work. So everything was done for what we were doing but we didn’t particular learn health & safety in the work place as such.

Interviewer:	Right. Okay. Have you had to do a lot of health and safety stuff since you’ve been at work?

Subject:	It’s always on your conscience; you make sure you’re wearing your safety boots and safety glasses and things. But I haven’t had to do any risk assessments. Anything I’ve done I’ve been shown the ones that have already been put in place but I haven’t done anything new, so I haven’t had to do anything like that.

Interviewer:	Okay. Do you think that the University could have done more to prepare you for the placement at all?

Subject:	Not really. Because so many people have gone with so many different companies, that it would have been impossible to prepare everyone. And basically if I wanted to learn more about the company I could have rung up and found out. So there’s nothing really the Uni could have done with the group as a whole.

Interviewer:	Okay. How have you found the transition from education to work? Has it been easy or difficult?

Subject:	Ah, it’s well easy because you don’t have to do any work when you get home. It’s great. You go to work 8 till 5. You go home and you don’t have to do anything.

Interviewer:	Yes. How has working all day been and getting up early and stuff like that?

Subject:	I work during the holidays anyway so it’s not really an issue for me.

Interviewer:	Okay, that’s great. Do you feel like you’ve had to face any new issues at all, like office politics or dealing with the boss and different types of people and stuff like that?

Subject:	Our bosses are great. They take in students for 15 years now so they know pretty much what we’re like and they’re really good if you’ve got an issue. If you got them and say I really don’t understand this, they’re really good at sitting down and explaining. They’ll take as much time as much time as you need. They’ve been great. You get a few office politics I guess but usually everyone just laughs about them.

Interviewer:	Yes. Are you looking forward to going back to Uni when you’ve finished?

Subject:	In a way and in a way not. (Yes.) It’ll be great to be back at Uni but it’s the whole back to your final year and the fact that you’re going to have to work really hard.

Interviewer:	What do you think are the main ways that work and University differ?

Subject:	At work you’ve got a lot more responsibility. At Uni you’re basically doing it to get marks aren’t you. (Yes.) And if you don’t do it then you don’t get any marks and that’s the end of it. Whereas here, if you don’t do it , it’s, you know, a multi-million pound project that you’re jeopardising in a way. Because it’s a very small group that I work in, there’s only eight people in it and three of us are students, we get a lot more responsibility than maybe other people would. Like, my boss is actually the project leader and he feeds stuff directly down to me, so we’re treated very much as members of the project team rather than a student.

Interviewer:	So you feel like you’re treated as permanent members of staff?

Subject:	Yes, definitely, but it comes with a responsibility.

Interviewer:	Yes. Do you think that University and work have got different goals in that sense then? Because you’re working towards a team effort, rather than …?

Subject:	Yes. At Uni you’re doing it for yourself basically, aren’t you? (Yes.) Sometimes you are as part of a group project but you know, if you pull out of that group project the others will carry on without you. (Yes.) But here you would be kind of dropping people in the deep end if you said well actually I’m not going to do that.

Interviewer:	Yes. Okay. We’ll talk a bit more about teamwork in a bit, but - How big is the company or the site that you’re working on?

Subject:	The site I’m on? About 500 staff maybe?

Interviewer:	Okay. Do they employ many women? In your team for instance?

Subject:	In my team there’s one other woman (inaudible). In general, to the actual engineering, science based divisions there probably aren’t that many women, but because it’s a mixed site and there’s stuff like, there’s a patent group, there’s an accountancy group, there’s marketing, there is overall quite a good ratio.

Interviewer:	Okay. You’re saying that the company is quite good place to be for placement students, because they’ve been having students for a long time and that. Do they have a particular structure or programme in place for you to follow, with targets or anything like that?

Subject:	Yes, we have like, when you start off you spend your first two months training and with us, one of last years students stayed over for a couple of weeks to show us the ropes and things, and we’ll do the same for the next guys. Basically after that you’re assigned to a project team or whatever and you do work for that project, but we have like quarterly reviews I think. I’ve had two anyway, to say, you know, what we’ve done well and if we feel that there’s something we really want to get involved in or whatever. Like I was doing a project and I took it through and we do a small scale R & D stuff and I said I’d really like to see what happens after. You know I’ve made this formulation, I’ve made this compound, what happens now? And they arranged for me to go over to materials division and see it being mixed and things.

Interviewer:	Yes. So you’re getting to see the whole process. But the company have been quite supportive of you doing things like that?

Subject:	Yes. I guess you review them (monthly?) but if we bring something like that up every day, they’ll do their best to sort it out for us. I mean obviously, after the compound’s made in Swindon they send it to Germany to actually be made into a product (inaudible) but they do what they can to help you out with things like that.

Interviewer:	Yes. Okay. Do you think that the structure for placement students could be improved at all? (Here?) Yes.

Subject:	Not really.

Interviewer:	Okay. Is the job that you’re doing what you expected or what you were told to expect prior to starting the placement?

Subject:	Yes, but only because I wasn’t sure what to expect. I rung up last year’s students and they told me. After I’d been for interview, we talked a bit about it on interview with the guys that was here last year and when I got offered the job I rung up again and said ‘what exactly did you do?’ so I chatted quite a while with Sonia who was here last year (inaudible) so I pretty much knew we’d been prepared for it. (Okay.) And this year, when we were interviewing next year’s students we made sure that we let them know.

Interviewer:	You were talking earlier about responsibility. Do you feel like you’ve been given an appropriate level of responsibility?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	Not too much or too little then?

Subject:	No. We do get responsibility, but if the pressure’s on someone will always help you out.

Interviewer:	So you’ve got the support systems in place to help you?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	Okay. How would you summarise your placement experience so far then?

Subject:	Really useful I guess. 

Interviewer:	What do you think have been the best and worst things about the placement?

Subject:	The best thing is generally seeing something you’ve made go - you know people are actually using that in the field now. I joined right at the end of one project and they had a last minute panic, and something I did, basically is now being used. So that’s really good. The worst things is that - I don’t know - it can get a bit repetitive just because of the nature of the job, you tend - if you’re testing something you tend to do two or three rounds of testing on the same thing, because you know you tweak it and you test it again. So it can get a bit boring but only for sort of two or three days. You don’t do the same thing constantly.

Interviewer:	What things do you think that you’ve gained from doing the placement?

Subject:	Just understanding work because it is so different from Uni. I think it’ll help me prepare for getting a job as a graduate as well. Things that I’ve seen - I know, like, how companies work, I’ve also seen, like, interviews, so - and I’ve interviewed people so I know more what people are looking for in an interview. That’s been really good actually, really enjoyed that. And also it’s quite specific here so I’ve gained a lot of knowledge about materials and I enjoy it, so I guess I’ve gained knowledge of what I’d like to do when I graduate.

Interviewer:	Okay. Do you think that there are any drawbacks to doing a placement, at all or do you think it’s all positive?

Subject:	It takes a year, so it’s a year that you’re not - you’re earning money but it’s not a graduate pay, whereas if you didn’t obviously you’d be earning more earlier. That’s about it really.

Interviewer:	Do you think that you have changed personally as a result of doing the placement?

Subject:	Yes I’m sure I have. We’ve all, like, matured and got more confident in doing things, but I don’t know if that’s within the work place. I don’t know if we take that home or not really.

Interviewer:	Okay. Do you think that you’ll use what you’re learning on placement in your final year?

Subject:	Yes. Definitely things like report writing has become like second nature because everything you do, you have to report back. So there’s that. You used to get a piece of like coursework and be ‘oh god I’ve got to write a report’ and now it’ll be do that in an hour sort of thing. You know the style and you learn a lot of tricks to make things easier.

Interviewer:	Do you have to do a final year project?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	Do you think you’ll use anything from work for that?

Subject:	Bits yes, but it depends what final year project I get, whether it’s related to this. The skills I’ve learned I’ll be able to transfer but the knowledge, it will depend what project I get.

Interviewer:	Okay. You said about there being other students on placement with you. How many students are there?

Subject:	In my group there’s two and there’s another two in sort of like a parallel group and we all live together.

Interviewer:	Are they people that you knew from [university]?

Subject:	One of them is. One of them is on my course.

Interviewer:	Okay. Do you think that all the students are treated equally?

Subject:	Within my division, yes. Obviously the guys in different divisions have got different bosses and things, but yes definitely.

Interviewer:	Do you think that it’s been an advantage or disadvantage having other students on placement with you then?

Subject:	An advantage I think. You’ve got somebody to bounce ideas off and if you’re not sure about anything you say, ‘what do you think about this?’ before you take it to someone else. We help each other out a lot as well, so if someone’s really got a lot of work on, you know, ‘what I’m doing isn’t high priority at the moment, do you want a hand?’

Interviewer:	Yes. Okay. Has your work involved a lot a teamwork?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	How do you think doing teamwork at work compares to doing teamwork at University? Have you found it easier, or more difficult?

Subject:	Sometimes it’s easier because there’s a company structure in place already. You’ve got a definite structure whereas at Uni it’s like someone’s picked to be team leader. They don’t necessarily have any more knowledge on it than you. Whereas here, the project leader is the guy who’s seen to have the most knowledge or the most skills in managing the team. So they’re a lot better at controlling it, diffusing situations and things like that.

Interviewer:	Do you think that other team members have clearer roles within the workplace than at University as well?

Subject:	Clearer roles?

Interviewer:	Like the work that you’re assigned within a project - does that make sense?

Subject:	Yes. Because you’re employed to do that job. Like the technicians are employed to do the technicians job so obviously they’re going to get the testing and the manufacturing guy is employed to do manufacturing so they get it. Whereas at university everyone’s on an equal ground. We’re on the same course, you’re working on the same module. If someone’s got a skill then you use it, but generally you’re all about the same.

Interviewer:	Okay. Do you think that the experience of doing teamwork at University helps you when you got to do teamwork in the workplace?

Subject:	Not particularly, just because I’ve done things outside Uni that have been team working as well. I’ve done a lot of sports etc. that I’d say probably helped more. And stuff like Duke of Edinburgh’s’ and stuff. I mean it probably has helped but not significantly.

Interviewer:	Is there anyone at work that you particularly liked or disliked working with?

Subject:	My boss is great. The other students are great. Then everyone has been really helpful, you know, guys in our division, guys in other divisions, everyone has been really good. If you’re having a problem or whatever … everyone’s good really.

Interviewer:	Okay. Have you been given a mentor at all in the company?

Subject:	Yes, he’s my boss.

Interviewer:	Okay. What do you think about that idea of mentoring?

Subject:	It doesn’t really make any difference to me because I see [name] on a day-to-day basis anyway and he’s my boss. If I’ve got a problem then I go to him first, as my boss rather than my mentor. I’ve never been in a situation where there’d be someone else who I’d rather see, and if there was – [name]’s the whole group boss and I could easily go to him as well.

Interviewer:	Okay. Why do you think that you’ve been given a mentor then, or what do you think the role of a mentor is?

Subject:	I’m assuming they’re meant to be there to sort out your problems and help you out with suggestions, but because of the way we’re treated day-to-day, we go through with other people.

Interviewer:	Okay. So is there anyone else that you go to for advice within the workplace, apart from your boss?

Subject:	My boss is [name] and [name] is basically on a parallel with him, he’s another project leader within the group and if [name]’s not here, [name] would be my next shout I guess. [name]’s been doing a course, the Six Sigma Course, so he’s been having like whole weeks off, but generally if there’s something I’m not quite sure about I can ask [name].

Interviewer:	Is there anyone in the company that you’d regarded a role model?

Subject:	In that I’d probably aspire to have sort of their job or level of responsibility, it would be [name] or [name]. I would like to be a project leader sort of thing. I’d enjoy that.

Interviewer:	Okay. Has anyone from university been to visit you on placement yet?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	Did you know the person?

Subject:	No.

Interviewer:	Do you think it would have been more useful if it was somebody you knew?

Subject:	If I was having problems, probably yes. But I’d already been here three months when he came, at least three months, probably four. And I was fine and basically he came and said yes, everything’s okay and you know, looked around and saw [other placement student] as well. But because everything was okay it didn’t really matter who he was.

Interviewer:	Okay. Did they talk to your manager as well?

Subject:	Yes. 

Interviewer:	Are you in contact with them or anyone else at University at other times? Are they there if you needed to talk to them?

Subject:	I’m sure they would be there if we needed them but I haven’t done.

Interviewer:	Okay. Do you know if there is a - either at University or at the work placement - is there a complaints procedure if you did have any problems?

Subject:	Yes, there is at work. I don’t know if there is at Uni.

Interviewer:	Okay. If you did have any problems, would you go to the University about it or would you try and sort it out yourself first?

Subject:	I’d just try and sort it out first. They’re quite reasonable here so I can’t see me having any problems that they’re not willing to sit down and help and talk about and stuff.

Interviewer:	Okay. Are there appropriate facilities for within your company, like if you have to have safety clothing and that, does it fit and things like that?

Subject:	Yes, lab coats are lab coats. They bought me safety boots that fit me and I could choose those and yes.

Interviewer:	Okay. Can you think of any occasions where you feel like your gender has determined reactions you’ve got from people and the outcome of any events at all?

Subject:	Only in ways that I’ve used it to my advantage.

Interviewer:	Okay. Like what?

Subject:	We’ve got a storeroom which is full of blokes who like, you know, they do welding and things. Generally if I go they’re nicer. So the lads will say ‘oh can you just pop down to the storeroom and ask for whatever’, generally because there aren’t many women around, I can persuade them and say oh yes.

Interviewer:	So they are more likely to get something done for you?

Subject:	Yes. They might just do it a bit quicker you know. But they do that for other people as well who are persuasive, so. I don’t know I might get different reactions from people but I don’t know what would happen if I was a bloke, so it’s hard to say.

Interviewer:	Okay. Do you want a career in engineering?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	Do you know what sort of area you want to go into yet?

Subject:	After this year, probably something like materials engineering, but I’m not sure yet.

Interviewer:	Do you think that you’d like a more managerial or technical role?

Subject:	Technical but in a project leading kind of way. So I want to be hands-on but I’d like to sort of have my own project to be hands-on in.

Interviewer:	Okay. Do you think that your career ambitions have changed as a result of doing the placement?

Subject:	In that I didn’t have any before. I still wanted to be hands-on before but now I know sort of what area I’d like to work in and things.

Interviewer:	Would you work for the company when you graduate, if you had the opportunity?

Subject:	If I had the opportunity, yes, but I’ve already asked and basically they won’t be taking anyone on. (Okay.) I’ve already tried that one.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the experience will help when you start working even if you enter a different field of engineering or a different area?

Subject:	Yes. I’m sure, but whatever I’ve learnt here will help wherever I go even if it’s not a materials place.

Interviewer:	Yes. Okay. I’ve nearly finished now. I’ve just got a few questions that I asked you in the previous interview. Not to test you to see if you get the same answers, but just to see if your opinion might have changed from your experiences. The first one is probably the hardest and that’s what five words would you use to describe the characteristics of your field of engineering?

Subject:	What five words would I use to describe the characteristics of my field of engineering?

Interviewer:	Yes. Your experience of engineering in the workplace?

Subject:	Fun. Material-based. Interesting. Challenging. Rewarding.

Interviewer:	Okay. 

Subject:	I bet I had none of those five words last time.

Interviewer:	Erm, no. Last time you said it was technical and hard-working.

Subject:	Oh, ok. I could have had hard working again.

Interviewer:	Would you say now that there are advantages or disadvantages to being a woman in engineering?

Subject:	There’s a bit of both. I’m sure in some places there’s probably disadvantages and I might have had disadvantages that I didn’t realise but I guess the advantages outweigh them. Even if just because people are looking to fill their ratio of women, you’re more likely to get an interview or whatever.

Interviewer:	Do you think that more women should be encouraged or enabled to do engineering then?

Subject:	If they want to, then they should be encouraged. But I wouldn’t say encouraging them to do it just because they’re women. But you have to want to do something otherwise there’s no point doing it.

Interviewer:	Yes. Do you think that it is an issue that there aren’t more female engineers?

Subject:	Not really. Obviously not lots of females want to be engineers, or there would be more. 

Interviewer:	Okay. That was everything, thank you very much.

You know I’ve made this formulation, I’ve made this compound, what happens now? And they arranged for me to go over to materials division and see it being mixed and things.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yes. So you’re getting to see the whole process. But the company have been quite supportive of you doing things like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes. I guess you review them (monthly?) but if we bring something like that up every day, they’ll do their best to sort it out for us. I mean obviously, after the compound’s made in Swindon they send it to Germany to actually be made into a product (inaudible) but they do what they can to help you out with things like that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yes. Okay. Do you think that the structure for placement students could be improved at all? (Here?) Yes.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Is the job that you’re doing what you expected or what you were told to expect prior to starting the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, but only because I wasn’t sure what to expect. I rung up last year’s students and they told me. After I’d been for interview, we talked a bit about it on interview with the guys that was here last year and when I got offered the job I rung up again and said ‘what exactly did you do?’ so I chatted quite a while with Sonia who was here last year (inaudible) so I pretty much knew we’d been prepared for it. (Okay.) And this year, when we were interviewing next year’s students we made sure that we let them know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You were talking earlier about responsibility. Do you feel like you’ve been given an appropriate level of responsibility?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Not too much or too little then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No. We do get responsibility, but if the pressure’s on someone will always help you out.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So you’ve got the support systems in place to help you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. How would you summarise your placement experience so far then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Really useful I guess.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you think have been the best and worst things about the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: The best thing is generally seeing something you’ve made go - you know people are actually using that in the field now. I joined right at the end of one project and they had a last minute panic, and something I did, basically is now being used. So that’s really good. The worst things is that - I don’t know - it can get a bit repetitive just because of the nature of the job, you tend - if you’re testing something you tend to do two or three rounds of testing on the same thing, because you know you tweak it and you test it again. So it can get a bit boring but only for sort of two or three days. You don’t do the same thing constantly.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What things do you think that you’ve gained from doing the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Just understanding work because it is so different from Uni. I think it’ll help me prepare for getting a job as a graduate as well. Things that I’ve seen - I know, like, how companies work, I’ve also seen, like, interviews, so - and I’ve interviewed people so I know more what people are looking for in an interview. That’s been really good actually, really enjoyed that. And also it’s quite specific here so I’ve gained a lot of knowledge about materials and I enjoy it, so I guess I’ve gained knowledge of what I’d like to do when I graduate.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Do you think that there are any drawbacks to doing a placement, at all or do you think it’s all positive?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It takes a year, so it’s a year that you’re not - you’re earning money but it’s not a graduate pay, whereas if you didn’t obviously you’d be earning more earlier. That’s about it really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that you have changed personally as a result of doing the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes I’m sure I have. We’ve all, like, matured and got more confident in doing things, but I don’t know if that’s within the work place. I don’t know if we take that home or not really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Do you think that you’ll use what you’re learning on placement in your final year?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes. Definitely things like report writing has become like second nature because everything you do, you have to report back. So there’s that. You used to get a piece of like coursework and be ‘oh god I’ve got to write a report’ and now it’ll be do that in an hour sort of thing. You know the style and you learn a lot of tricks to make things easier.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you have to do a final year project?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think you’ll use anything from work for that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Bits yes, but it depends what final year project I get, whether it’s related to this. The skills I’ve learned I’ll be able to transfer but the knowledge, it will depend what project I get.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. You said about there being other students on placement with you. How many students are there?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: In my group there’s two and there’s another two in sort of like a parallel group and we all live together.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are they people that you knew from [university]?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: One of them is. One of them is on my course.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Do you think that all the students are treated equally?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Within my division, yes. Obviously the guys in different divisions have got different bosses and things, but yes definitely.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that it’s been an advantage or disadvantage having other students on placement with you then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: An advantage I think. You’ve got somebody to bounce ideas off and if you’re not sure about anything you say, ‘what do you think about this?’ before you take it to someone else. We help each other out a lot as well, so if someone’s really got a lot of work on, you know, ‘what I’m doing isn’t high priority at the moment, do you want a hand?’

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yes. Okay. Has your work involved a lot a teamwork?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How do you think doing teamwork at work compares to doing teamwork at University? Have you found it easier, or more difficult?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Sometimes it’s easier because there’s a company structure in place already. You’ve got a definite structure whereas at Uni it’s like someone’s picked to be team leader. They don’t necessarily have any more knowledge on it than you. Whereas here, the project leader is the guy who’s seen to have the most knowledge or the most skills in managing the team. So they’re a lot better at controlling it, diffusing situations and things like that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that other team members have clearer roles within the workplace than at University as well?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Clearer roles?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Like the work that you’re assigned within a project - does that make sense?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes. Because you’re employed to do that job. Like the technicians are employed to do the technicians job so obviously they’re going to get the testing and the manufacturing guy is employed to do manufacturing so they get it. Whereas at university everyone’s on an equal ground. We’re on the same course, you’re working on the same module. If someone’s got a skill then you use it, but generally you’re all about the same.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Do you think that the experience of doing teamwork at University helps you when you got to do teamwork in the workplace?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not particularly, just because I’ve done things outside Uni that have been team working as well. I’ve done a lot of sports etc. that I’d say probably helped more. And stuff like Duke of Edinburgh’s’ and stuff. I mean it probably has helped but not significantly.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is there anyone at work that you particularly liked or disliked working with?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: My boss is great. The other students are great. Then everyone has been really helpful, you know, guys in our division, guys in other divisions, everyone has been really good. If you’re having a problem or whatever … everyone’s good really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Have you been given a mentor at all in the company?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, he’s my boss.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. What do you think about that idea of mentoring?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It doesn’t really make any difference to me because I see [name] on a day-to-day basis anyway and he’s my boss. If I’ve got a problem then I go to him first, as my boss rather than my mentor. I’ve never been in a situation where there’d be someone else who I’d rather see, and if there was – [name]’s the whole group boss and I could easily go to him as well.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Why do you think that you’ve been given a mentor then, or what do you think the role of a mentor is?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’m assuming they’re meant to be there to sort out your problems and help you out with suggestions, but because of the way we’re treated day-to-day, we go through with other people.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. So is there anyone else that you go to for advice within the workplace, apart from your boss?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: My boss is [name] and [name] is basically on a parallel with him, he’s another project leader within the group and if [name]’s not here, [name] would be my next shout I guess. [name]’s been doing a course, the Six Sigma Course, so he’s been having like whole weeks off, but generally if there’s something I’m not quite sure about I can ask [name].

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is there anyone in the company that you’d regarded a role model?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: In that I’d probably aspire to have sort of their job or level of responsibility, it would be [name] or [name]. I would like to be a project leader sort of thing. I’d enjoy that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Has anyone from university been to visit you on placement yet?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you know the person?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it would have been more useful if it was somebody you knew?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: If I was having problems, probably yes. But I’d already been here three months when he came, at least three months, probably four. And I was fine and basically he came and said yes, everything’s okay and you know, looked around and saw [other placement student] as well. But because everything was okay it didn’t really matter who he was.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Did they talk to your manager as well?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are you in contact with them or anyone else at University at other times? Are they there if you needed to talk to them?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’m sure they would be there if we needed them but I haven’t done.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Do you know if there is a - either at University or at the work placement - is there a complaints procedure if you did have any problems?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, there is at work. I don’t know if there is at Uni.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. If you did have any problems, would you go to the University about it or would you try and sort it out yourself first?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’d just try and sort it out first. They’re quite reasonable here so I can’t see me having any problems that they’re not willing to sit down and help and talk about and stuff.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Are there appropriate facilities for within your company, like if you have to have safety clothing and that, does it fit and things like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, lab coats are lab coats. They bought me safety boots that fit me and I could choose those and yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Can you think of any occasions where you feel like your gender has determined reactions you’ve got from people and the outcome of any events at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Only in ways that I’ve used it to my advantage.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Like what?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: We’ve got a storeroom which is full of blokes who like, you know, they do welding and things. Generally if I go they’re nicer. So the lads will say ‘oh can you just pop down to the storeroom and ask for whatever’, generally because there aren’t many women around, I can persuade them and say oh yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So they are more likely to get something done for you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes. They might just do it a bit quicker you know. But they do that for other people as well who are persuasive, so. I don’t know I might get different reactions from people but I don’t know what would happen if I was a bloke, so it’s hard to say.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Do you want a career in engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you know what sort of area you want to go into yet?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: After this year, probably something like materials engineering, but I’m not sure yet.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that you’d like a more managerial or technical role?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Technical but in a project leading kind of way. So I want to be hands-on but I’d like to sort of have my own project to be hands-on in.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Do you think that your career ambitions have changed as a result of doing the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: In that I didn’t have any before. I still wanted to be hands-on before but now I know sort of what area I’d like to work in and things.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you work for the company when you graduate, if you had the opportunity?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: If I had the opportunity, yes, but I’ve already asked and basically they won’t be taking anyone on. (Okay.) I’ve already tried that one.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the experience will help when you start working even if you enter a different field of engineering or a different area?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes. I’m sure, but whatever I’ve learnt here will help wherever I go even if it’s not a materials place.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yes. Okay. I’ve nearly finished now. I’ve just got a few questions that I asked you in the previous interview. Not to test you to see if you get the same answers, but just to see if your opinion might have changed from your experiences. The first one is probably the hardest and that’s what five words would you use to describe the characteristics of your field of engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: What five words would I use to describe the characteristics of my field of engineering?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yes. Your experience of engineering in the workplace?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Fun. Material-based. Interesting. Challenging. Rewarding.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I bet I had none of those five words last time.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Erm, no. Last time you said it was technical and hard-working.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh, ok. I could have had hard working again.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you say now that there are advantages or disadvantages to being a woman in engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: There’s a bit of both. I’m sure in some places there’s probably disadvantages and I might have had disadvantages that I didn’t realise but I guess the advantages outweigh them. Even if just because people are looking to fill their ratio of women, you’re more likely to get an interview or whatever.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that more women should be encouraged or enabled to do engineering then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: If they want to, then they should be encouraged. But I wouldn’t say encouraging them to do it just because they’re women. But you have to want to do something otherwise there’s no point doing it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yes. Do you think that it is an issue that there aren’t more female engineers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not really. Obviously not lots of females want to be engineers, or there would be more.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. That was everything, thank you very much.
